ParseBench

 
 
 
 
 
 

 New: ParseBench 2 — 4,317 test cases in six dimensions (now with forms), scored with
 severity-aware metrics. Run it with parse-bench run --dataset parsebench-2 .

 Related: For schema-guided enterprise document extraction, see our companion benchmark ExtractBench.

 ParseBench is a benchmark for evaluating how well document parsing tools convert PDFs into structured output that AI agents can reliably act on. It tests whether parsed output preserves the structure and meaning needed for autonomous decisions — not just whether it looks similar to a reference text.

The original benchmark (ParseBench v1) covers 2,000 human-verified pages from real enterprise documents (insurance, finance, government), organized around five capability dimensions, each targeting a failure mode that breaks production agent workflows. ParseBench 2 extends it with more pages, a forms dimension and metrics that score each error using human-aligned severity classes.

 
 
 

 ParseBench 2

ParseBench 2 combines broad coverage of real-world documents with metrics calibrated to how much each error matters:

- Six dimensions. Text, formatting, tables, charts, layout (visual grounding) and the new forms dimension, with 600 form pages.
- Severity-aware scoring. A page score is the lower of a content-recovery score and a severity cap, so recovering most of a page cannot hide a serious error — a changed number, a flipped negation, swapped table headers or a misread form value. Changes between supported formats that keep the same information cost nothing.
- Calibrated against stated priorities. The metrics are tuned against 330 controlled scenarios in six severity test suites, each with a target score drop (critical, major, minor or harmless), and check for over 140 error types.
- 4,317 page-level test cases from 2,645 documents. The revised ParseBench v1 pages, with more complete answer keys (every chart has its full data table), plus targeted datasets of hard cases: complex table headers, financial, insurance and dense tables, headings, strikeout, underline and government forms.

One command downloads the dataset to ./data parsebench-2 , runs a pipeline on every subset and writes the six dimension scores and the overall score to output/parsebench-2/ score/ / next score.json :

 

The overall score is the unweighted mean of the six dimensions. Within a dimension, page scores are averaged per dataset and the datasets are combined with fixed weights, so collecting more pages for one capability does not give it more influence:

 Dimension Datasets ( --group name) Cases Metric 
 --- --- ---: --- 
 Text text 508 text next 
 Formatting text (3/4), headings (1/8), strikeout (1/16), underline (1/16) 508 + 353 formatting v2 
 Tables tables (1/2), complex table headers , financial tables , insurance filing tables , dense tables (1/8 each) 1,753 table next 
 Charts charts 568 chart next 
 Layout layout 535 layout grounding pass rate 
 Forms forms (7/8), fillable forms (1/8) 600 forms v2 

To score outputs from your own parser, write them in the ParseBench results layout and run parse-bench evaluation run --next=SUBSET=RESULTS DIR::TEST CASES DIR,... --next only ( --next only skips the ParseBench v1 metrics, which the ParseBench 2 score does not use). ParseBench 2 scores are not comparable with ParseBench v1 scores.

intro.html:
New: ParseBench 2 — 4,317 test cases in six dimensions (now with forms), scored with severity-aware metrics. Run it with parse-bench run <pipeline> --dataset parsebench-2.

Related: For schema-guided enterprise document extraction, see our companion benchmark ExtractBench.

ParseBench is a benchmark for evaluating how well document parsing tools convert PDFs into structured output that AI agents can reliably act on. It tests whether parsed output preserves the structure and meaning needed for autonomous decisions — not just whether it looks similar to a reference text.

The original benchmark (ParseBench v1) covers ~2,000 human-verified pages from real enterprise documents (insurance, finance, government), organized around five capability dimensions, each targeting a failure mode that breaks production agent workflows. ParseBench 2 extends it with more pages, a forms dimension and metrics that score each error using human-aligned severity classes.

install.title: Quick Start
install.html:
Prerequisites: Create a .env file with the API key for the parsing tool you want to evaluate (see Configuration for details).

# Install from PyPI (pick the extras for the providers you want to run)
pip install "parse-bench[runners]"          # every provider SDK
pip install "parse-bench[llamaparse]"       # or just one, e.g. llamaparse / openai / anthropic / google

# Or, from a checkout of this repo
uv sync --extra runners

# Optional: add the `fast` extra for a JIT-accelerated TEDS table metric (numba).
# Scores are identical to the default path — just faster on large tables.
pip install "parse-bench[runners,fast]"

# Quick test run (small dataset, 3 files per category — good for trying things out)
# (drop the `uv run` prefix if you installed from PyPI)
uv run parse-bench run llamaparse_agentic --test

# Full benchmark run (replace llamaparse_agentic with any pipeline name, see "Available Pipelines" below)
uv run parse-bench run llamaparse_agentic

# ParseBench 2: all 13 subsets, scored into six dimensions and an overall score
uv run parse-bench run llamaparse_agentic --dataset parsebench-2

# View interactive reports in your browser
uv run parse-bench serve llamaparse_agentic

usage.title: Usage
usage.html:
Running the Benchmark

The run command runs inference (calls the parsing tool), evaluates the results against ground truth, and generates reports:

# Evaluate a parsing tool on all five dimensions
uv run parse-bench run <pipeline_name>

# Evaluate on a single dimension only (e.g., chart, table, layout, text_content, text_formatting)
uv run parse-bench run <pipeline_name> --group chart

# Skip calling the parsing tool — just re-evaluate existing results
uv run parse-bench run <pipeline_name> --skip_inference

# Control how many pages are processed in parallel
uv run parse-bench run <pipeline_name> --max_concurrent 10

# Run on the small test dataset only (3 files per category, good for trying things out)
uv run parse-bench run <pipeline_name> --test

When running all dimensions, the benchmark produces:

  • Per-dimension detailed HTML reports with drill-down per test case
  • An aggregation dashboard showing all dimensions side-by-side
  • A leaderboard comparing all evaluated tools in the output directory
  • CSV, Markdown, and JSON exports per dimension
Viewing & Comparing Results
# View reports in your browser (needed because browsers block PDF rendering from file:// URLs)
uv run parse-bench serve <pipeline_name>

# Compare two parsing tools side-by-side
uv run parse-bench compare <pipeline_a> <pipeline_b>

# Generate a leaderboard across all evaluated tools
uv run parse-bench leaderboard

# Leaderboard for specific tools only
uv run parse-bench leaderboard llamaparse_agentic llamaparse_cost_effective
Advanced Subcommands

For fine-grained control over individual steps:

# Run inference only (call the parsing tool, don't evaluate)
uv run parse-bench inference run <pipeline_name>

# Run evaluation only (on existing inference results)
uv run parse-bench evaluation run --output_dir ./output/<pipeline_name>

# Generate detailed HTML report from evaluation results
uv run parse-bench analysis generate_report --evaluation_dir ./output/<pipeline_name>

# Regenerate the aggregation dashboard
uv run parse-bench analysis generate_dashboard --evaluation_dir ./output/<pipeline_name>
Evaluating Your Own Tool

To add a new parsing tool to ParseBench, use Claude Code:

/integrate-pipeline <name> <API docs or SDK link>

This creates the provider, registers the pipeline, and updates docs. The skill definition lives in .claude/commands/integrate-pipeline.md and can be adapted for other AI coding agents.
